name: Jade Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'll be honest, that's easier than being careful.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Corbel Facilities, a maintenance company, and I'm based on a contract covering four office blocks, a leisure centre and a doctors' surgery in town. My day is changing lights, testing emergency lighting, checking that appliances are safe, and going out to whatever's broken, usually with Dev, the senior electrician. I log every job on a tablet, which I used to hate and now don't mind. I like the variety, and the leisure centre staff are lovely, but I'm tired of being the junior who gets sent up the tallest ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I could believe that, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it wasn't the big deal people said. I'd post a joke about it maybe. At work I'd say the tablet is still slow, so no change there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's not AI that's hurting us, it's robots that are already here. My boyfriend's parcel depot already brought in sorting robots last year, and his overtime vanished. For us, the robots aren't a story, they're a smaller payslip. So I'm not calm, even if nothing new happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Corbel, because my job's fine as long as the contract renews in March. I'd move 30 a week into savings now that Kai's overtime is gone, so we've got a buffer. I'd ask Dev if I can start shadowing him on the inspection reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's okay, our money is tight, and Kai's depot keeps changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the Corbel contract doesn't renew in March?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Corbel might move me to another contract an hour away, or let me go. There aren't many maintenance firms around here. I try not to think about it until February.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did Kai take losing the overtime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kai was quiet for a week, then he started doing a few Saturday shifts at his cousin's car wash. He says it's fine. I can see it isn't, because he's tired all the time.

say: I'd say AI **wasn't the big deal** people claimed.
I'd joke at work that the **tablet** is still slow.
think: Kai's depot brought in **sorting robots** last year and his overtime vanished.
Our worry comes from **robots already here**, not new AI.
do: Keep going at Corbel while the **contract renews** in March.
Move **30 a week** into savings to make up for Kai's lost overtime.
Ask Dev if I can shadow him on **inspection reports**.
feel: Uneasy: my job's okay, but our **money is tight**.
S0.quote: My boyfriend's parcel depot already brought in sorting robots last year, and his overtime vanished. For us, the robots aren't a story, they're a smaller payslip.
fieldNote: The household already feels **automation** through her boyfriend's depot.
Her own job depends on a **contract renewal** she avoids thinking about.
She moves **step by step**: shadowing, saving, no big leaps.

steps.text: Keep working the Corbel contract through the March renewal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first. Like the reporting I do on the tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for paperwork, and tradespeople should still be fine. I'd say that to friends at least. I'd tell people at work to learn the new tools once they're proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it hits Corbel through the buildings, not through me. Half our contract is keeping the lights on in office blocks. If the offices are half empty, the company that maintains them needs half the electricians. And Kai's depot would get even more robots, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever reporting app Corbel brings in, once Dev has tried it. I'd keep saving the 30 a week. Kai and I would put off moving to a bigger flat for a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not dramatic, it's like a slow leak in the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said wait until Dev has tried it. Why not jump in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the last app Corbel brought in lost a week of my logs. I'm not against change, I just let somebody else find the bugs. Dev's good at that, he moans about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would putting off the bigger flat mean for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're in a one-bed with Kai's bike in the hallway, and we'd talked about getting a dog. That would wait. It's small, but it's the stuff that makes you feel like life's moving.

say: I'd say AI makes sense for **paperwork**, and trades should be fine.
I'd tell colleagues to learn new tools once they're **proven**.
think: Corbel is hit through the **buildings**: fewer office workers, fewer electricians.
Kai's depot keeps adding **robots** slowly, which could cut his hours further.
do: Learn Corbel's new **reporting app** after Dev has tested it.
Put off moving to a **bigger flat** for two years.
feel: Anxious, like a **slow leak** in the roof.
S1.quote: Half our contract is keeping the lights on in office blocks. If the offices are half empty, the company that maintains them needs half the electricians.
fieldNote: She sees the threat through **emptier offices** rather than her own tasks.
She waits for proof because the last app **lost her logs**.
Small life plans, like a **dog** and a bigger flat, get delayed.

steps.text: Learn Corbel's reporting app once Dev has tried it
Stay in the one-bed flat and delay getting a dog

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots in 2031. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is moving faster than anyone can cope with. I'd say the government should step in with some support. I wouldn't be shouting, though, I'd be too busy worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd both lose our jobs within five years. In the fast version, my boyfriend's depot goes first and my job goes three years later. Two hands-on jobs, one household, no savings. I'd be 31 and starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything we can: Kai's car, eating out, the phone upgrades. I'd apply to the hospital's own maintenance team, because hospitals will be careful about robots. I'd tell my mum we might need her spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can picture the letter from Corbel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the letter say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like, due to changes in how our clients use their buildings, your role is at risk. Dev would keep his job longer because he signs things off. I'd be first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that thinking AI in 2028 would change in your own day before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tablet stuff, the reports and booking jobs, would all be done for me. Honestly, that would free me up to do more actual electrics for a couple of years. It's just that Corbel might use it to need fewer of us.

say: I'd say this is **too fast** for anyone to cope with.
I'd call for **government support**, but quietly.
think: Kai's depot goes **first** and my job goes **three years later**.
I'd be **31** and starting again with no savings.
do: **Cut** Kai's car, eating out and phone upgrades.
Apply to the **hospital's maintenance team**, where robots arrive more carefully.
Ask my mum about her **spare room**.
S2.quote: In the fast version, my boyfriend's depot goes first and my job goes three years later. Two hands-on jobs, one household, no savings.
fieldNote: She expects **both incomes** to go within five years.
She looks for a **careful employer** like a hospital as shelter.
Thinking AI would ease her **paperwork** but could shrink the team.

steps.text: Sell Kai's car and stop eating out
Apply to the hospital's in-house maintenance team
Ask Mum about moving into her spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Robots in 2034. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if people start now. I'd say get your licence and get into places that need people, like hospitals and schools. I'd say it to my cousin, who's just started an apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I had a chance. Five years is enough to get a licence and move into hospital maintenance, where nobody lets a robot near the operating theatre wiring without a person signing it off. Kai would need a plan too, and that's harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the licence next autumn, after asking two people who've done it which college is best. I'd keep saving 30 a week, and push it to 40 when I qualify. I'd help Kai look at forklift and depot maintenance roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but hopeful. Five years is enough to do one big thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the hospital in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I did a week covering the surgery's electrics and everything had to be signed off twice. Places like that move slowly on purpose. Slow is good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Kai do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kai likes machines, so maybe he'd train to fix the depot's robots instead of working next to them. He'd need someone to push him. That'd be me.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** if people start now.
I'd tell my cousin to get into places that **need people**, like hospitals.
think: Five years lets me get a **licence** and move into **hospital maintenance**.
Kai needs a plan too, and that's **harder**.
do: Sign up for the **licence** next autumn after asking two people who've done it.
Save **30 a week**, rising to 40 once qualified.
feel: Anxious but **hopeful**, with time for **one big thing**.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to get a licence and move into hospital maintenance, where nobody lets a robot near the operating theatre wiring without a person signing it off.
fieldNote: She sees **careful employers** like hospitals as slower to automate.
She checks with **people who've done it** before choosing a college.
She takes charge of **Kai's plan** as well as her own.

steps.text: Enrol in the licence course next autumn
Save 30 a week, rising to 40 once qualified
Help Kai apply for depot robot maintenance training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels a lot more manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time, so people shouldn't panic. I'd tell friends to get qualified and save while things are normal. I'd probably say it online too, for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine if I'm sensible. With ten years' warning, I'd rather be the electrician checking the robot's work than the one racing it. By 2039 I'd be 40 and hopefully a senior on a hospital contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the licence, then an inspection and testing course a couple of years later. I'd keep working at Corbel until I've got the hospital experience. Kai and I would get the bigger flat and the dog, but save a bit more first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. I'd still keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get the dog after all. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means we can live a normal life for a while. With two years I'd freeze everything. With ten, I'd plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, oddly. Dev is 50 and he'd be near retirement when the robots come, which sounds fine, but he hates learning new things. He'd be bitter if they changed the job under him.

I'd tell friends to **get qualified** and save while things are normal.
think: I'd rather **check the robot's work** than race it.
By **2039** I'd hope to be senior on a hospital contract.

Stay at Corbel until I've got **hospital experience**.
Get the **bigger flat** and the dog after saving a bit more.
feel: Uneasy but **okay**, still keeping an eye on it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Kai and I would both be in hands-on jobs with nothing saved. What would help is paid training for couples like us, so one of us can study while the other works. People talk about AI like it's coming for lawyers. In our flat, it's already taken my boyfriend's overtime and it might take my contract next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the people already living with robots. Everyone talks about the future, but Kai's depot is the present.

headlineQuote: People talk about AI like it's coming for lawyers. In our flat, it's already taken my boyfriend's overtime and it might take my contract next.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old junior** on a maintenance contract for offices and a surgery.
She uses AI **now and then**, waiting for colleagues to prove new tools first.
Her household already feels automation through boyfriend Kai's **parcel depot**.
Fast AGI **alarms** her because both their hands-on jobs could go within five years.
With more time, she plans a **licence** and hospital maintenance work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both her and Kai in hands-on jobs and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training for couples**, so one can study while the other works.
